been so endemic for so long.

of it's changed just

- Hello everyone.
Welcome to the "Altium OnTrack" podcast.
I'm very happy today to be speaking

with Dr. John W. Mitchell,
president and CEO of IPC.
John has been on several times before
and I'm always very happy to talk to him.

We've talked to him about
events IPC has going on
in the past, and of course,
the recent release of one of his books.

And I'm very happy to talk to
him today about IPC Apex 2025.

John, thank you so much
for being here today.
- My pleasure. Thanks for having me, Zach.
- So a lot has been going on
in the industry the last few years,

I mean, between CHIPS Acts
and ultra high density

and reshoring, nearshoring,
all of this stuff going on.
But I think it all kind

of converges at this one event
each year, which is IPC Apex.

So if you could, please give
us the rundown of IPC Apex
and really why folks should care.
- Sure.
So IPC Apex Expo is North America's
largest electronics manufacturing event.

We bring together professionals
from across the industry,

from designers to engineers,
manufacturers, suppliers,

and it lets them really
showcase the latest advancements

in PCB design, fabrication,
assembly, test, and inspection.
The show also attracts a global audience,

serves as a critical
platform for innovation,
education and business growth
in the electronics manufacturing industry.
It's really kind of three shows in one.
You've got the expo, which is, you know,
where people are showing their wares.
You've got the technical conferences

where a lot of learning and
information exchange happens.
Then you have the standards efforts
as well, going on all at the same time.
- Yeah if you look at the program,

I noticed that it was kind
of like three shows in one.

And I have to admit, I've
never been to IPC Apex, so.
- Oh, you gotta come, Zach. Come on.
(Zach laughing)
- Well, I tried to-
- It's just down the street.

- Yeah, well for me it is
'cause I'm in Portland.

- It is for you.
- And it's in Anaheim,
so it's a very short plane ride for me.
And I did notice it is, as you described,
like three shows in one,

because you've got
standards committees meeting
for some important standards work
at the beginning of the week.

Then you've got a pretty
expansive expo that lasts,

I think three days and then
kind of littered between that,
you've got some technical sessions.

So it seems like there's
a lot going on there

and, you know, someone can
really make a whole week
out of it if they want to.
- Definitely. Yeah.
Some of the standards meetings,

as you mentioned, start
as soon as Saturday
before the main event

and then run all the way
through the following Saturday.

And then technical
conference stuff begins,

I believe around Tuesday
and runs through, actually,

I think some may actually
run into Friday as well,

but anyway, mainly Tuesday,
Wednesday, Thursday.

And same with the expos
Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday.

- So if you could, tell
the folks out there,
why they should attend IPC Apex

because there's quite a few
big shows that happen each year

and I think it's probably
difficult for folks
to prioritize a couple of those to go to.

So why should IPC Apex be
up at the top of their list?

- Yeah, so IPC Apex
Expo is good to come to
because it brings all of it together.
And so, you know, it brings professionals

from across the electronics
manufacturing ecosystem.

The exhibition hall features
the latest advancements
and access to cutting edge technologies,

from leading capital
equipment manufacturers
as well as product innovators.
And you get to see the innovations

and get hands-on
demonstrations as well as, too,
you can compare products
and services from literally hundreds
of exhibitors across one roof.

And as you mentioned, the
standards meetings, you know,
if you're looking to, you know,
IPC sets the global standards
for electronics design and manufacturing.
So attending standards committee meetings
allows participants to actually contribute

to the industry's future and
to make their voices heard.

There's also great
networking opportunities.

We have, not quite 10,000 people
that come out to the event,

but there's powerful
networking opportunities

from various receptions
and informal meetings.

You get, like I mentioned,
all different types,

whether you're a designer,
an industry leader,
an executive, really, it opens the door

for collaboration, partnerships
as well as career growth.

And then finally, you
know, if you're looking
to advance your career or gain new skills
or expand your business opportunities,
because it is three shows in one,
you can really do all of that at once.

And it gives you access to
the decision makers as well

as key players from
across the supply chain.

- Now you mentioned the
standards committees
and the standards committees are one area

where I think some designers
may feel it's a bit opaque.
They probably wonder,

how do people get involved
in the standards committee,

how do they select, you know,
what goes into a standard

and how do they select who
even gets to participate?

So tell us a bit more about
the standards committees,

and what's the process for
people who wanna get involved?
- Sure. It's very complex.
You have to fill out 173 page form
in triplicate by hand in cursive.
No, I'm just kidding.
You just have to have an interest.
If you have an interest and a desire
and hopefully something relevant.
We don't just want, you know, people
that are interested in basket weaving,

showing up at, you know,
a wrong kind of standard.
But go, come, there are open meetings.
We invite everybody to come.
And the only limitation is when it comes
to voting is there's only one vote
per company that can happen.

So there's a certain
company delegate that gets
to vote on behalf of the standard

to see whether they're
adopted by the industry.
But literally anybody can come.
If you're sitting there going,

"Well, I don't understand
the standard," get involved!
We'd love to have you.
- So someone can literally just show up
and sit in the office.
- You can show up.

- For a standards meeting.
- That's right.

- Okay.
- And say, hey,
here's this standard,

I'm interested in figuring
out this design thing

or this, you know, assembly
piece or whatever it may be,
communication standard on industry 4.0.

And you say, "Hey, there's a
standard going on about this.
I'd love to go in."
And then you can walk into the meeting

and be part, listen, pay
attention and ask questions.
- Now that's really interesting

because I have participated
in standards groups,
but not with IPC.
So I've done it with ANSI and IEEE.
And that's really interesting
because those standards meetings
and the activities are really closed off.
You know, you have to kind of be admitted
through peer review, if you will.
Whereas it sounds like this, you know,
it's a totally different process.
- So there is not a peer review to enter,

but if you're going to make
your case, people need to know
that you know what you're talking about.
- [Zach] Well, sure.
- We actually get evaluated by ANSI

to make sure we're following
the ANSI processes.

And so like I was talking
about, you know, coming in

and talking about something
that's off the wall

or not having the understanding
of it is not really
what we're looking for there.

But we encourage even
young engineers to come in
'cause it's a great learning opportunity

and asking those questions helps
you progress in your career

as well as find other
mentors that, you know,
we actually marry that up into

and through our emerging
engineer program as well.

- Yeah, and I'm sure this
gives some companies,

an opportunity to maybe
push their innovations

into a standard or, you
know, in front of people
who are responsible for incorporating
that information into a standard as well.

- Yeah, we do try to make sure
that proprietary information,
you know, it needs to be freely available
if it's gonna become part of a standard.

So we don't standardize
somebody's proprietary technology.
Most people don't want that anyway.

But what we do do is
take great data sources

and then the committees are
able to utilize, you know,

leverage that, look at it, and
then make comments around it

and make sure that the proper
specifications are adopted.
- Sure, sure.

So going back to the whole show
just for a moment, you know,
IPC, obviously a standards organization.
I think a lot of the understanding

of the standards is focused
around manufacturing
or probably designed for manufacturing.

And so I think it's fair that
some folks might view IPC Apex
as only a conference for manufacturers.
Is that true or is there something here
for electronics designers as well?
- Oh, absolutely.
So on the design front,
I knew you were gonna ask this,

so I pulled up, there's
all kinds of sessions
and meetings specifically on PCB design

and emerging trends in next
generation PCB technologies

that will help as well
as system level design

and transforming the landscape
of modern electronics.
So there's like a design town hall meeting
that happens in the middle
of the conference so people can be heard.

There's professional development
courses covering design,
and I think there's four

technical conference side.
It looks like there's 12

like designed for high speed,

high bandwidth reliability,
designed to scale,

advanced packaging and
EV power electronics,
things like that.

There's the standards
committee meetings in terms

or the DFX standards committee
and printed board additive

So lots of things that are
either directly tied to design

or specifically relevant
to design as we go forward.
- Yeah.
- There's six other additional committees,

covering design as
well, so a lot of stuff.
- Yeah, yeah, obviously.

And listening to you
read through that list,
you mentioned a couple of of areas
that I think are still emerging.

And so it sounds like designers
really have an opportunity
to kind of get in on the best information
and learn what they need to learn
before they make that step.
- Yeah, if you're gonna be involved
in electric vehicle power electronics
or advanced packaging pieces,

things like that, you're
gonna wanna be there.
- Absolutely. Absolutely.

So some of the technical
courses obviously centered

around design, but what else
is there for manufacturing?

Are there like types of
courses that are for people

who are interested in
getting into manufacturing,

like process engineering,
those types of things?

there's like 32 different
professional development courses.

They cover things like cleaning
a cleanliness bootcamp.
There's an additive manufacturing,
solder mask coating portion,
polymers and advanced packaging,
sustainable surface finishes for UHDIs,
course on counterfeit electronics.
Well, I don't know if designers,

nobody ever in a design front

Then there's, you know, advanced
packaging, assembly tests,

design, electronics assembly,
emerging technologies,
factory of the future,
like industry 4.0, PCB fabrication, HDI,
UHDI and substrates,

power electronics,
automotive high voltage,

quality and reliability,
sustainability, you name it.
There's just all kinds of tracks

much anything to do

with electronics from
the conceptualization
of it all the way through to, you know,
it being put in a box and put on a shelf.
- Okay.

normally when we say technical conference,

we're referring to like, for
example, companies presenting,

what would typically
be like a paper, right?
They're probably presenting research,
they're probably presenting innovations.
Do we also have that over there as well?
- There are those as well.

- Okay. (laughs) So it's
not just professional.

- So yeah, there's like
scientific paper competitions

develop or learn various pieces

the electronics, how to

international presence,

we're trying to reinforce
global collaboration
in electronics manufacturing

We put more focus on the
workforce development,
like we've been talking about,
helping companies address the skills gap

soon as you hire somebody,
the skill gap has started to widen

We've embraced industry
4.0, AI automation,
advanced materials, making it a hub

There's been increased engagement

HDI, what we would think
